solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Rubbish celebrity almost securing a great deal

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the last letter of the word is dropped
to secure something is to hold it fast, so one piece is held inside the other

blocks.note: fame, or celebrity, with its final letter cut
lots is a large amount

explanation.surface: Someone dismisses a celebrity as rubbish just as they are about to land a lucrative contract.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rubbish' reads like a verdict on the celebrity, but it is the definition; the trimmed fame wraps around lots.
explanation.definitionFit: Flotsam is floating wreckage and debris, and by extension any worthless junk or discarded odds and ends.

clue.text: Gradually tire going round clubs after a show

indicators.note: to go round something is to surround it, so one piece encloses another
after places one piece directly behind another in the sequence

blocks.note: to fade is to lose strength gradually
taken as written
C is the abbreviation for clubs in card games

explanation.surface: A performer's stamina slowly flags as they tour the clubs after one big show.
explanation.walkthrough: Clubs comes after a, giving AC, and FADE goes round that pair to make FACADE.
explanation.definitionFit: A facade is an outward appearance put on to mislead, a pretence, which is what a show means here.

clue.text: Huge tail of distinct, brightly coloured bird

indicators.note: a tail is the very end of something, so only the final letter of the word is kept

blocks.note: OS is the abbreviation for outsize, used on clothing labels
the closing letter of distinct
rich colours are deep and vivid

explanation.surface: A large bird is admired for its huge, vividly coloured tail.
explanation.walkthrough: OS for outsize is a standard clothing-size abbreviation that crosswords use for huge.
explanation.definitionFit: The ostrich is a large flightless African bird, the biggest living species, so it is simply an example.

clue.text: Empty container in a prison redesigned for waste material

indicators.note: emptying a word takes out its contents, leaving only its outer letters
something redesigned is rebuilt to a new plan, so the letters are rearranged
in places one piece inside another

blocks.note: the first and last letters of container
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: An empty shipping container is placed in a prison that has been redesigned to handle waste.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged A PRISON gives S-APIRON, and the emptied container slips in after the S.
explanation.definitionFit: Scrap iron is discarded metal kept for reprocessing, a kind of industrial waste material.

clue.text: Head of state on the radio

indicators.note: anything heard on the radio is only spoken, so a word that sounds the same is wanted

blocks.note: Maine is a state in the north-east United States

explanation.surface: A head of state gives an address over the radio.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head of state' looks like one phrase for a president; split it, and Head is the definition while state is the American state.
explanation.definitionFit: Head as an adjective, as in head office, means chief or principal, which is what main means.

clue.text: Backsliding British publication went ahead and took risks

indicators.note: sliding backwards means moving in the reverse direction, so the letters run right to left

blocks.note: B is the abbreviation for British
a mag, or magazine, is a publication
to lead is to go in front

explanation.surface: A wayward British magazine pressed on regardless and took chances.
explanation.walkthrough: Mag is short for magazine; only the first two pieces turn round, while the final verb follows unchanged.
explanation.definitionFit: To gamble is to bet or to act on a chance of loss, so the past tense matches took risks.

clue.text: Sandwich possibly good, certainly with large filling

indicators.note: with simply adds one piece alongside the next
a filling sits inside something, so one piece goes into another

blocks.note: G is the abbreviation for good
of course is an emphatic yes
L is the abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: Someone judges a sandwich: probably good, and definitely generously filled.
explanation.walkthrough: Sandwich is a town in Kent whose Royal St George's links has hosted the Open; the capital is hidden by the sentence start. L fills OF COURSE after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Sandwich is a well-known example of a championship golf links, hence the qualifier possibly marking it as one instance.

clue.text: Decent mark on exam

blocks.note: M is an abbreviation for mark, the old German currency
an oral is a spoken examination

explanation.surface: A respectable grade is awarded for a test.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mark on exam' reads as a grade, but mark is the abbreviation M and the exam is an oral.
explanation.definitionFit: A moral person is ethical and principled, so decent works as an adjectival synonym.

clue.text: Forget about that bird trapped among bricks!

indicators.note: something trapped among other things is surrounded by them, so one piece sits inside another

blocks.note: Lego is the toy building-brick brand
a tit is a small songbird

explanation.surface: Someone tells a worrier to stop fretting about a bird that got stuck in a pile of bricks.
explanation.walkthrough: The small bird sits inside the toy-brick name, splitting it after LE.
explanation.definitionFit: Let it go is a spoken idiom urging someone to stop dwelling on something, the same as saying forget about it.

clue.text: Plans to assist lifting some weight

indicators.note: in a down entry lifting raises the letters, so they read bottom to top

blocks.note: to aid is to help
grams are units of weight

explanation.surface: A gym has schemes to help members lift heavier weights.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lifting some weight' sounds like gym work, but lifting turns the help word upward in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Plans as a noun are technical drawings showing layout, which is exactly what diagrams are.

clue.text: Provide food, support and help with moving things?

blocks.note: to cater is to supply food
a pillar holds a structure up

explanation.surface: A removals or events firm offers catering, back-up and help shifting furniture.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a playful definition: not the insect, but the caterpillar track on heavy vehicles.
explanation.definitionFit: Caterpillar tracks are continuous belts that let tractors and tanks move heavy loads, a whimsical stretch marked by the question mark.

clue.text: Drink in the bar regularly

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is kept

blocks.note: the first, third and fifth letters of these words

explanation.surface: Someone orders their usual drink at the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the bar' sounds like where you drink; 'in' is a link and the letters come from the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Tea is a hot beverage made by infusing leaves, so it is an example of a drink.

clue.text: Silly Republican in daft clothing?

indicators.note: clothing covers what it is worn by, so one piece wraps around another

blocks.note: dippy is informal for foolish
R is the abbreviation for Republican

explanation.surface: A foolish Republican politician turns up in ridiculous clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clothing' reads as a noun for daft outfits, but as a verb it has the daft word dress the Republican.
explanation.definitionFit: Drippy is British slang for feeble, wet or sentimental, and so foolish in a weak way.

clue.text: Artist is corrupt and about to steal lead from churches

indicators.note: turning about means facing the other way, so the letters run backwards
stealing takes something in, so a letter is taken inside the group
the lead of a word is its front, so only the opening letter is kept

blocks.note: to rot is to decay or corrupt
plus means and
the opening letter of churches

explanation.surface: A crooked artist is about to strip the lead from church roofs.
explanation.walkthrough: Stealing lead from church roofs is a real crime, so 'about to steal' reads as intent; in fact about is the turn signal and 'and' stands for its arithmetic synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: A sculptor makes three-dimensional works in stone, metal or clay, one particular kind of artist.

clue.text: Measure beat in heart

indicators.note: in places one piece inside another

blocks.note: the heart of something is its centre
musical time is the beat

explanation.surface: A doctor checks the rhythm of a patient's heartbeat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beat in heart' suggests a pulse, but beat is musical time sitting inside the middle word; the spelling is British.
explanation.definitionFit: A centimetre is a metric unit of length, one hundredth of a metre, so it is a measure.

clue.text: So her fancy meal has scope for fungus

indicators.note: fancy means elaborate or ornamental, so the letters are worked into a new pattern

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
mush is soft pulpy food
room means space or scope

explanation.surface: A woman's elaborate dinner leaves room for a mushroom dish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancy meal' wants to be one phrase; fancy works only on the two opening words, and meal stands alone.
explanation.definitionFit: The horse mushroom is a large edible wild species, Agaricus arvensis, so it is an example of a fungus.

clue.text: Paths made around an area of London

indicators.note: something made around is put together in a turned-about way, so the letters are shuffled

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Footpaths have been laid out around a district of London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Made' looks like part of the indicator alone, but it is also fodder alongside paths.
explanation.definitionFit: Hampstead is a district of north London known for its heath, so it is an instance of a London area.

clue.text: Crim stirred up trouble over some LSD

indicators.note: stirring mixes things up, so the letters are jumbled
turned over means upside down, so in this down entry the letters run backwards

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
a to-do is a fuss or commotion

explanation.surface: A criminal caused a disturbance involving some LSD.
explanation.walkthrough: Crim is informal for a criminal; 'stirred up trouble' reads as one phrase but splits after up.
explanation.definitionFit: A microdot is a tiny pill containing a dose of LSD, so it is a portion of the drug.

clue.text: Very insignificant thing featuring in terribly asinine film

indicators.note: something featuring in a work appears inside it, so one piece goes into another
terribly means very badly, so the letters are badly scrambled

blocks.note: it is a pronoun for a thing
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A trivial object appears in a dreadfully silly movie.
explanation.walkthrough: The small word goes inside the rearranged letters; the clue reads as a film review.
explanation.definitionFit: Infinitesimal means immeasurably tiny, so it describes something extremely slight or negligible.

clue.text: Money paid to host one political group in Pretoria, as intended

indicators.note: a host takes in guests, so one piece holds others inside

blocks.note: a fee is a payment for a service
I is the Roman numeral one
the African National Congress, South Africa's ruling party

explanation.surface: A payment is made to accommodate a South African political party, as was planned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As intended' reads like 'as planned', but intended is a noun here; Pretoria is South Africa's capital, hence the ANC.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone's intended is the person they are engaged to marry, an old-fashioned noun use matching fiancée.

clue.text: Hide from everyone at first in state of agitation

indicators.note: at first points to the beginning, so only the opening letter is taken
in places one piece inside another

blocks.note: to be in a lather is to be worked up
the opening letter of everyone

explanation.surface: Someone first hides from everybody while in a panic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hide' reads as a verb, but it is the noun for an animal skin.
explanation.definitionFit: Leather is tanned animal skin, and a hide is the skin of an animal, especially once treated.

clue.text: Media magnate tries acquiring Time

indicators.note: acquiring something means gaining it as an extra, so a piece is added on

blocks.note: a judge hears, or tries, a case
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A media mogul attempts to buy Time magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: Time with its capital looks like the magazine, but it is just T; tries is the courtroom sense.
explanation.definitionFit: William Randolph Hearst was the American newspaper publisher who built a vast press empire, the model for Citizen Kane.

clue.text: Again accept when to open an American’s CV

indicators.note: to open something is to get inside it, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: a résumé is the US term for a CV
as can mean when, as in 'as he left'

explanation.surface: Someone takes on the job of reviewing an American candidate's CV again.
explanation.walkthrough: A CV, or curriculum vitae, is what Americans call a résumé.
explanation.definitionFit: To reassume is to take up or take on again, so accepting a role a second time fits.

clue.text: Mark ignores final part of suspect letter from overseas

indicators.note: to ignore something is to leave it out, so a letter is dropped
the final part is the very end, so only the last letter is picked out

blocks.note: a stigma is a mark of disgrace
the closing letter of suspect

explanation.surface: A postmark overlooks the end of a suspicious letter sent from abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Letter from overseas' suggests mail, but it is an alphabet letter, here a Greek one; the T leaves the disgrace word.
explanation.definitionFit: Sigma is the eighteenth letter of the Greek alphabet, so it is a character used in a foreign script.

clue.text: A number of houses close to collapse, say

indicators.note: the close of something is its end, so the last letter is taken

blocks.note: the closing letter of collapse
to state is to say

explanation.surface: Several houses are said to be on the verge of falling down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Close to collapse' reads as nearly falling, but it means the last letter of collapse.
explanation.definitionFit: A housing estate is a planned development of many homes built together, so a group of dwellings.

clue.text: School somehow managed with power cut

indicators.note: cut means removed, so a letter is taken out

blocks.note: to cope is to manage, somehow, under difficulty
P is the abbreviation for power

explanation.surface: A school got by somehow during a power cut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Power cut' reads as a blackout, but cut removes the P from the coping word.
explanation.definitionFit: A co-ed is a co-educational school teaching boys and girls together, a common noun use in Britain.

clue.text: Bones from fish turned over

indicators.note: turning over flips something round, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: the cod is a common sea fish

explanation.surface: Fish bones turn up when a fillet is flipped over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bones from fish' is a natural phrase; Bones is the definition, slang for a doctor.
explanation.definitionFit: Sawbones, shortened to Bones, is old slang for a surgeon, and doc is an informal word for a doctor.

clue.text: Party guest leaving us to collect that lady

indicators.note: when something is leaving it goes away, so those letters are taken out

blocks.note: guest without the pair of letters U and S
taken as written
to collect someone is to go and get them
her is the pronoun for that woman

explanation.surface: A party guest leaves the group to fetch a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Us' is fodder for the deletion, taken literally from guest, not a pronoun for the solver.
explanation.definitionFit: A get-together is an informal social gathering, a casual synonym for a party.

clue.text: Identical signatures always primarily included in TV intro music?

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so the opening letters are taken
included in places one piece inside another

blocks.note: a theme tune opens a television show
the opening letters of these two words

explanation.surface: A TV show's opening music always seems to share the same signature tune.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Signatures' suggests key signatures in music, but only its first letter is used.
explanation.definitionFit: The same means not different in any way, which is what identical means as a predicate adjective.

clue.text: Accomplished revolutionary ripped apart French philosopher

indicators.note: a revolution is a turning round, so the letters are reversed

blocks.note: did means carried out
tore is the past tense of tear

explanation.surface: A skilled revolutionary demolished a French thinker's arguments.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' wants to be RED, but here it signals a turn; the ripped word is turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: Denis Diderot was an Enlightenment thinker and chief editor of the Encyclopédie, a famous example of a French philosopher.
